content.text: Electric Charges and Fields
1.1 Electric Charge
All of us have the experience of seeing a spark or hearing a crackle when we take off our synthetic clothes or sweater, particularly in dry weather.
Another common example of electric discharge is the lightning that we see in the sky during thunderstorms.
Electrostatics deals with the study of forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges. Static means anything that does not move or change with time.
Historically, the credit of discovery of the fact that amber rubbed with wool or silk cloth attracts light objects goes to Thales of Miletus, Greece, around 600 BC.
There are two kinds of electrification: (i) like charges repel and (ii) unlike charges attract each other. The property which differentiates the two kinds of charges is called the polarity of charge.
The charges were named as positive and negative by Benjamin Franklin. By convention, the charge on glass rod rubbed with silk is positive; that on plastic rod rubbed with fur is negative.
1.2 Conductors and Insulators
Conductors: charges flow freely through them. Metals (copper, aluminium, silver), human and animal bodies, earth.
Insulators: charges do not flow. Glass, rubber, plastic, wood, porcelain, nylon.

Free charge carriers
Charge flows easily
Metals, electrolytes, earth
Used in wiring, circuits
1.4 Basic Properties of Electric Charges
Quantisation
Charge exists in discrete packets, not continuous.
q = ne
n = integer (0, ±1, ±2, …)
e = 1.602192 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (magnitude of electron/proton charge)
At the macroscopic level (e.g., 1 μC contains ~10¹³ electronic charges), quantisation has no practical consequence. At the microscopic level (tens or hundreds of e), quantisation cannot be ignored.
1.5 Coulomb's Law

Coulomb measured the force between two point charges and found that it varied inversely as the square of the distance between the charges and was directly proportional to the product of the magnitude of the two charges.
\vec{F}_{21} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{r_{21}^2} \hat{r}_{21}

Coulomb used a torsion balance to measure force between charged metallic spheres. The charges were unknown initially. His clever method: put a charged sphere in contact with an identical uncharged sphere — by symmetry, each gets q/2. Repeat to get q/4, etc.
Coulomb's Law: F = k|q₁q₂|/r². Like gravity, it's an inverse-square law — but unlike gravity, it can be attractive or repulsive.
The ratio of electric force to gravitational force between a proton and an electron is approximately 10³⁹. Electric force is vastly stronger.
1.7 Electric Field
Action at a distance is hard to conceptualise. We introduce an intermediary — the field. A charge creates a field around it. Another charge placed in that field experiences a force.
\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{Q}{r^2} \hat{r}
\vec{F} = q\vec{E}

(i) The source charge Q must remain at its original location. The test charge q should be negligibly small so it doesn't disturb Q.

(ii) E⃗ is independent of the test charge q — it depends only on the source charge and position.

(iii) For positive source charge, E⃗ points radially outward. For negative, radially inward.
1.13 Gauss's Law
The total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to 1/ε₀ times the net charge enclosed by the surface.
\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}
Gauss's Law: ∮ E⃗ · dA⃗ = q/ε₀. The power is in choosing the right Gaussian surface — symmetry is everything.
Examples

If 10⁹ electrons move out of a body every second, how much time is required to get 1 C on the other body?

Charge per second: 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 10⁹ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ C/s
Time = 1 C ÷ (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ C/s) = 6.25 × 10⁹ s ≈ 198 years
One coulomb is a very large unit. A 1 cm³ piece of copper contains about 2.5 × 10²⁴ electrons.

props.title: Example 1.2 — Charge in a Cup of Water

content.text:
How much positive and negative charge in 250 g of water?

Molecules = (250/18) × 6.02 × 10²³. Each molecule has 10 electrons + 10 protons.
Total charge = (250/18) × 6.02 × 10²³ × 10 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.34 × 10⁷ C
Summary
Electric and magnetic forces determine the properties of atoms, molecules and bulk matter.
Two types of charges: positive and negative. Like charges repel, unlike attract.
Coulomb's Law: F = k|q₁q₂|/r², k ≈ 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
Gauss's Law: ∮ E⃗ · dA⃗ = q/ε₀. Based on inverse-square law.
